emails.subject: URGENT: Your password expires in 30 minutes
emails.preview: Your account password is about to expire. Verify now to avoid being locked out.
emails.bodyHtml:
Dear Team Member,

Our security system has detected that your corporate account password is set to expire in 30 minutes.

To maintain uninterrupted access to your email, files, and company applications, you must verify your identity immediately using the link below.

Reset Password Now →

⚠️ Failure to complete this within 30 minutes will result in your account being permanently locked. You will need to appear in person with photo ID to regain access.

If you believe you received this in error, contact IT Support at ext. 5555.

IT Security Team
Corporate Help Desk — Ticket #IT-20489
emails.explanation: This is a phishing email. The sender is not from your company's real IT domain, and the reset link secretly points to a Russian (.ru) domain — not your company's login page.
evidence: Sender domain is 'corp-itsupport.net', not your company's domain
The link displays 'login.company.com' but actually goes to 'corp-verify.ru'
Extreme urgency and threats ('permanently locked', 'appear in person') are classic pressure tactics
Legitimate IT teams never send unsolicited password resets via email

emails.subject: Confidential – Urgent wire transfer needed today
emails.preview: Need you to process a transfer to a new vendor before EOD. Keep this confidential.
emails.bodyHtml:
Hi,

I'm currently in back-to-back meetings and can't call. I need you to process an urgent wire transfer of $47,500 to a new vendor we're onboarding for the Q1 partnership deal.

This is time-sensitive and needs to clear by end of day. Please handle this immediately and keep it confidential for now — I'll explain the full context at tomorrow's all-hands.

Bank details:

  • Bank: First Meridian Trust
  • Account: 8821045593
  • Routing: 021000021
  • Reference: ACME-Q1-VENDOR

Once done, please reply to confirm and do not discuss this with anyone else in the office. Appreciate your quick action on this.

Marcus Webb
Chief Executive Officer, Acme Corporation
(Sent from mobile)
emails.explanation: This is a Business Email Compromise (BEC) attack — one of the most costly types of fraud. The attacker impersonates your CEO using a lookalike domain to trick you into wiring money.
evidence: Sender domain is 'acme-executives.net' — not 'acme.com'
Real executives don't email employees directly to request unauthorized wire transfers
The secrecy demand ('keep this confidential', 'don't discuss with anyone') is a major red flag
Urgency + a request to bypass normal approval processes is a hallmark of BEC fraud
Always verify large financial requests via a phone call to the known number
